name: Interview probability, set 4
description: Probability questions interviewers ask: stopping, coupons, indicators, Bayes, waits, flies, sticks, tags, truels, games, totals and Kelly. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.prose: Roll a fair twelve-sided die, faces 1 to 12, and be paid the face in pounds. You may roll up to three times. After each of the first two rolls you either stop and take that face or roll again. You must keep the third roll.
items.question: What is the game worth with the best rule, in pounds? Give two decimal places.

widget.accept: £8.83, which is 53/6: keep 9 or more on the first roll and 7 or more on the second.
widget.label: Value in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Value the last roll first, then work back one roll at a time.

byKey.two-rolls: You valued the game with two rolls. A third roll in hand makes the first roll pickier: keep only 9 or more.
byKey.one-roll: You never rolled again. A low first roll is worth less than the rolls still to come.
byKey.first-vs-fresh: You kept 7 or more on the first roll, comparing it with one fresh roll. Two rolls are left, worth £8, so keep only 9 or more.
byKey.best-of-three: You kept the best of three rolls. Once you roll again, the earlier face is gone.

explain.text: One roll is worth 6.5, so with two rolls keep 7 or more: 0.5 × 9.5 + 0.5 × 6.5 = 8. With three rolls, keep a first roll only if it beats 8. That gives (4/12) × 10.5 + (8/12) × 8 = 53/6 ≈ £8.83.

items.prose: A fair spinner has seven equal sectors, and each spin costs you £1.20. You keep spinning until every sector has come up at least once. Then you collect a prize of £30.
items.question: What is your expected profit, in pounds? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split the wait into stages, one for each new sector, and price the spins.

byKey.seven-spins: You paid for seven spins, one per sector. Repeats are common, so the wait is 18.15 spins on average.
byKey.forty-nine: You paid for 49 spins, seven for each sector. Each new sector is a geometric wait: 7/7, 7/6, and so on.
byKey.skip-first: You left out the first spin. It always shows a new sector, but you still pay for it.

explain.text: With k sectors seen, a new sector takes 7/(7 − k) spins on average. The stages add to 7(1 + 1/2 + ⋯ + 1/7) = 18.15 spins. They cost 1.2 × 18.15 = £21.78, so the profit is 30 − 21.78 = £8.22.

items.prose: Twelve balls are thrown at random into eight boxes. Each ball lands in any box with chance 1/8, independently of the others.
items.question: How many boxes do you expect to stay empty? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Give each box a 0 or 1 marker for staying empty, then add the expectations.

byKey.one-box: You found the chance that one box stays empty. Add that chance over all 8 boxes.
byKey.filled: You counted the boxes that get at least one ball. Take that from 8 for the empty ones.
byKey.eighth-power: You raised 7/8 to the number of boxes. A box stays empty only if all 12 balls miss it.

explain.text: Give each box an indicator: 1 if it stays empty. A box is missed by all 12 balls with chance (7/8)¹² ≈ 0.2014. Adding the 8 indicators gives 8 × 0.2014 ≈ 1.61, even though they depend on each other.

items.prose: A fraud screen flags 90% of bad accounts and 8% of good ones. 2% of accounts are bad. An account is flagged by two independent runs of the screen.
items.question: What is the chance the account is bad? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the base rate as odds and multiply by the ratio of flag rates once per flag.

byKey.one-screen: You used one flag. The second independent flag multiplies the odds by 11.25 again.
byKey.no-base: You left out the 2% base rate. Bad accounts start rare, at odds of 2 to 98.
byKey.sens-squared: You gave the chance that a bad account is flagged twice. The question asks the reverse.

explain.text: The odds start at 2 to 98. Each flag multiplies them by 0.9/0.08 = 11.25, so two flags give 253.125 to 98. The chance is 253.125/351.125 ≈ 0.7209.

items.prose: Three independent alarms each go off after an exponential wait. Their rates are 2, 3 and 5 an hour.
items.question: How long do you expect to wait for the first alarm, in minutes?

widget.accept: 6 minutes: the first of them has rate 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 an hour.
widget.label: Minutes

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance that all three alarms are still silent after a time t.

byKey.mean-of-means: You averaged the three mean waits. The first alarm comes sooner than any one of them on average.
byKey.fastest-only: You took the fastest alarm alone. The other two can still go off first.
byKey.add-means: You added the mean waits. That is longer than waiting for all three in turn, not the first.
byKey.avg-rate: You averaged the rates. Rates of independent alarms add, so use 10 an hour.

explain.text: The first alarm waits past t only if all three do: e^(−2t) × e^(−3t) × e^(−5t) = e^(−10t). So the first wait is exponential with rate 10 an hour. Its mean is 1/10 of an hour, which is 6 minutes.

items.prose: Two trains are 120 miles apart on one track and head towards each other at 40 mph each. A fly leaves the front of one train at 90 mph. It flies to the other train, turns back, and keeps going until the trains meet.
items.question: How far does the fly travel, in miles?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find how long the fly is in the air before adding up any legs.

byKey.one-train: You used one train's speed for the gap. The trains close at 80 mph, so they meet after 1.5 hours.
byKey.gap: You gave the gap between the trains. The fly is faster than either train and keeps turning back.
byKey.meeting-point: You gave the distance each train covers. The fly moves at 90 mph the whole time.

explain.text: The trains close at 40 + 40 = 80 mph, so they meet after 120/80 = 1.5 hours. The fly flies at 90 mph all that time. It covers 90 × 1.5 = 135 miles, with no series to add.

items.prose: A stick 60 cm long is broken once, at a point chosen uniformly along it.
items.question: What is the expected length of the longer piece?

options.why: You found the expected length of a piece chosen at random. The longer piece is never under 30 cm.
You took the larger of two independent lengths up to 60 cm. The two pieces add to 60, so they are not independent.
That is the longest of three pieces from two breaks, 11/18 of the stick. Here there is one break.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the longer piece as max(X, 60 − X) and ask how it is spread.

explain.text: The break X is uniform on 0 to 60, and the longer piece is max(X, 60 − X). It is uniform on 30 to 60, because X and 60 − X give the same length. So its mean is (30 + 60)/2 = 45 cm.

items.prose: A researcher tags 50 fish in a lake and lets them go. A week later she catches 40 fish, and 8 of them carry tags.
items.question: What is the usual estimate of the number of fish in the lake?

widget.accept: 250: 8 in 40 is a fifth, so the 50 tags are a fifth of the lake.
widget.label: Fish in the lake

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Assume the catch holds the same share of tagged fish as the lake.

byKey.flipped: You turned the ratio upside down. The tagged share of the catch, 8/40, should match 50 over the whole lake.
byKey.seen-only: You counted only the fish you have handled. The lake holds many that were never caught.
byKey.catch-ratio: You scaled the catch instead of the tags. Multiply the 50 tagged fish by 40/8.

explain.text: Tagged fish make up 8/40 = 1/5 of the catch. If the catch is typical, the 50 tagged fish are 1/5 of the lake. So the estimate is 50 × 5 = 250 fish.

items.prose: Three players fight a truel. A hits with chance 0.4, B with 0.7, and C never misses. They fire in turn A, B, C, skipping anyone who is out, until one is left. B and C each aim at the other, the stronger rival.
items.question: What should A do with the first shot?

options.text: Fire into the air: A then wins with chance about 0.46
Aim at C: A then wins with chance about 0.34
options.why: You aimed at the best shooter. If A hits, A faces B in a duel and B fires first.

options.text: Aim at B: A then wins with chance about 0.28
options.why: You aimed at B. If A hits, C fires next and never misses.

options.text: It makes no difference: A wins with chance 0.4 whatever A does
options.why: You took A's hit rate as A's chance. A's target decides whom A faces next and who fires first.

feedback.correct: Correct. Firing into the air is best.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Value each first move by the duel it leads to and who fires first in it.

explain.text: After an air shot, B hits C with chance 0.7, and A fires first at B. Otherwise C hits B, and A has one shot at C. A wins 0.7 × 0.4/0.82 + 0.3 × 0.4 ≈ 0.461, more than 0.335 for aiming at C.

items.prose: Forty counters sit on a table. Two players take turns to remove 1, 2 or 5 counters. Whoever takes the last counter wins. You move first.
items.question: How many counters should you take on your first move?

widget.accept: Take 1 and leave 39, a multiple of 3.
widget.label: Counters to take

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work up from small piles and mark the ones that lose for the player to move.

byKey.mod-six: You used the rule for takes of 1 to 5, which leaves a multiple of 6. Here 3 and 4 are not allowed.
byKey.most: You took the most you could. That leaves 35, and your opponent takes 2 to leave 33.
byKey.two: You left 38. Your opponent takes 2 and leaves 36, a multiple of 3.

explain.text: Piles of 0, 3 and 6 lose for the player to move. Takes of 1, 2 or 5 never move a multiple of 3 to another multiple of 3. So from 40, take 1 to leave 39.

items.prose: Three fair dice are rolled. You learn that they total 12 and that the first die shows a 4.
items.question: What is the chance that the other two show a 3 and a 5, in either order? Give four decimal places or a fraction.

widget.accept: 2/5 = 0.4: 2 of the 5 equal pairs that make 8.
widget.label: Chance

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the rolls that agree with everything you know, then count inside them.

byKey.one-order: You counted (3, 5) but not (5, 3). Either order counts.
byKey.whole-table: You divided by all 36 pairs. Only the pairs that total 8 are still possible.
byKey.forgot-first: You used all 25 rolls that total 12. The first die is known to show 4, which leaves 5.
byKey.no-double: You left out (4, 4). A double four also makes 8, so there are five pairs, not four.

explain.text: With the first die at 4, the other two must total 8. Five ordered pairs do that, all equally likely. Two of them are (3, 5) and (5, 3), so the chance is 2/5 = 0.4.

items.prose: You bet again and again at evens on a coin that wins with chance 0.62. The Kelly fraction is 0.62 − 0.38 = 0.24 of your bankroll. A colleague stakes 0.48 of the bankroll on every bet instead.
items.question: What is the expected log growth per bet at a stake of 0.48?

options.text: Slightly negative, about −0.005: the bankroll shrinks in the long run
About +0.029, the same as at the Kelly fraction
options.why: You took the growth at the peak. Past 0.24 the growth falls away.

options.text: About +0.058, twice the growth at the Kelly fraction
options.why: You doubled the growth with the stake. A bigger stake adds variance, which drags log growth down.

options.text: Exactly zero, as the parabola rule says
options.why: You used the quadratic rule of thumb. The log hurts more on losses than it helps on wins, so the exact value is below zero.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out 0.62 ln(1 + f) + 0.38 ln(1 − f) at f = 0.48.

explain.text: The growth is g(f) = 0.62 ln(1 + f) + 0.38 ln(1 − f). At f = 0.48 it is 0.62 × 0.3920 + 0.38 × (−0.6539) ≈ −0.0054. Twice Kelly cancels the growth roughly, and the exact log tips it below zero.
